etymology: From the narrative of John 9; the man blind from birth whom Christ healed and who confessed Him.
biblical_def: The man born blind is the subject of the ninth chapter of John, blind from his birth, whom the Lord Jesus healed by anointing his eyes with clay and sending him to wash in the pool of Siloam. When the disciples asked whose sin had caused his blindness, his own or his parents’, the Lord answered that neither, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him—teaching that not all affliction is the fruit of particular sin, and that God ordains suffering for the display of His glory. The healed man, brought before the Pharisees, grew bolder as they grew more hostile: he confessed that Jesus was a prophet, reasoned that one who opened the eyes of a man born blind must be of God, and, cast out of the synagogue, worshipped Christ when the Lord revealed Himself as the Son of God. His progress from sight of the body to sight of the soul is one of Scripture’s clearest pictures of conversion, while the Pharisees, claiming to see, were declared blind in their sin. The dictionary honors this narrative as a parable of spiritual sight given by sovereign grace, and as the Lord’s own word that the worst blindness is that of those who say, We see, yet will not come to the light.
webster_summary: The man blind from birth healed in John 9; a picture of spiritual sight given by grace, who grew bolder in confessing Christ as the Pharisees grew blind in unbelief.

corruption_summary: The healing is read as a lesson against linking sin and suffering at all, or reduced to a mere social parable; in truth it displays sovereign grace and the blindness of unbelief.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One misreading takes the Lord’s words—neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents—to deny any link between sin and suffering whatever, as though no affliction ever flowed from particular sin. The text says no such thing; it teaches that this man’s blindness was not so caused, that the works of God might be displayed in him (John 9:3). The Lord corrects a presumptuous reading of providence, not the truth that sin and the curse stand behind all suffering.

The principle to recover is that spiritual sight is the sovereign gift of God and that the gravest blindness is that of the self-assured. The healed man, simple and unlettered, confessed what he knew—one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see (John 9:25)—and was led on to worship Christ as the Son of God (John 9:38). The learned Pharisees, claiming sight, were pronounced blind because they would not come to the light (John 9:39). Grace opens the eyes of the helpless; pride seals the eyes of the proud.
roots_summary: From John 9; the man blind from birth healed by Christ, a picture of spiritual sight given by grace over against the blindness of unbelief.

etymology: Aramaic talitha qumi, Damsel, arise; the words of Christ raising the daughter of Jairus (Mark 5:41).
biblical_def: Talitha cumi are the Aramaic words of the Lord Jesus, preserved by Mark and interpreted in the text itself, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise, spoken as He took by the hand the dead daughter of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue. Jairus had fallen at Jesus’ feet, beseeching Him to heal his little daughter who lay at the point of death; while He yet spake, word came that the child was dead, and the mourners laughed Him to scorn when He said she only slept. But the Lord put them all out, took the father and mother and three disciples, and spoke the word that even death obeys: and straightway the damsel arose and walked. The keeping of the very Aramaic syllables marks an eyewitness memory, the tender words of the Lord ringing in the ear of Peter who told them to Mark. The scene displays the Lord’s power over death itself, His tenderness toward a grieving father and a little child, and His sovereign word that calls the dead to rise as easily as a mother wakes a sleeping child. The dictionary honors talitha cumi as a window into the compassion and omnipotence of Christ, a foretaste of the resurrection morning, when at His voice all that are in the graves shall come forth.
webster_summary: The Aramaic words of Christ, Damsel, arise, by which He raised the dead daughter of Jairus; a display of His tender power over death.
webster_full: TALITHA CUMI, Aramaic for Damsel, arise (Mar 5:41).

Jairus, a synagogue ruler, had fallen at Jesus’ feet for his dying child.

The kept Aramaic marks an eyewitness memory, told by Peter to Mark.

corruption_summary: The raising is explained away as a mere awakening from a coma; the text and the scorn of the mourners testify that the child was truly dead and truly raised.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the rationalist explaining away of the miracle: that the child was not truly dead but in a swoon or coma, and that Jesus merely roused her. But the text resists this. Word came that she was dead (Mark 5:35); the professional mourners had already gathered; and they laughed Him to scorn when He said she slept, knowing well that she was dead (Mark 5:40). The Lord’s word that she slept is the language of resurrection faith, not a medical diagnosis—the same way He called dead Lazarus asleep.

The principle to recover is the sovereign power of Christ over death. He bade the grieving father, Be not afraid, only believe (Mark 5:36), and then proved His word by calling the dead child to rise with a phrase as gentle as a mother waking her daughter. This power is not a relic of one ancient miracle; it is the pledge of the last day, when all that are in the graves shall hear His voice and come forth (John 5:28). Talitha cumi is the whisper of the resurrection morning, when the same Lord shall raise His people incorruptible.

etymology: From raise + dead; the restoration of the dead to life by the power of God in Christ.
biblical_def: The raising of the dead is the restoration of those who have died to life again by the power of God, wrought through prophets and apostles as His instruments and, supremely, by the Lord Jesus Christ in His own person and authority. The Old Testament records that Elijah and Elisha raised the dead; the Gospels record three raised by Christ—the daughter of Jairus, the widow’s son at Nain, and Lazarus four days in the grave—and the Acts record Peter raising Dorcas and Paul restoring Eutychus. These raisings, however, were restorations to this mortal life, from which those raised would die again; they are signs and pledges, not the final resurrection. The Lord Jesus is Himself the resurrection and the life, and His own rising from the dead, never to die again, is the firstfruits and guarantee of the great resurrection at the last day, when He shall call all that are in the graves, the just unto the resurrection of life and the unjust unto the resurrection of damnation. The dictionary honors the raisings of Scripture as displays of the Lord’s dominion over death and as foretastes of that final morning, distinguishing carefully between these temporary restorations and the bodily, glorious, and unending resurrection of the saints in Christ.
webster_summary: The restoration of the dead to life by God’s power; the raisings by prophets, Christ, and apostles, signs and pledges of the final resurrection at the last day.
webster_full: RAISING OF THE DEAD, restoration of the dead to life by God’s power.

Christ raised Jairus’ daughter, the widow’s son, and Lazarus.
These were restorations to mortal life, not the final resurrection.
Pledges of the last day, when all in the graves shall hear His voice.
scriptures: Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:

corruption_summary: The raisings are reduced to legend or confused with the final resurrection; Scripture distinguishes these temporary signs from Christ’s deathless rising and the last-day resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One corruption dismisses the raisings of Scripture as legend or misunderstanding; another, more subtly, blurs them into the final resurrection, as though Lazarus rose as the saints shall rise. Both err. The raisings were real, attested, and wrought by the power of God; yet they were restorations to this mortal life, from which Lazarus and the rest died again. They are signs of Christ’s dominion over death, not the deathless glory of the last day.

The principle to recover is the distinction between these temporary raisings and the resurrection of which Christ is the firstfruits. The Lord is Himself the resurrection and the life (John 11:25); His own rising, never to die again, is the firstfruits and pledge of them that slept (1 Cor 15:20). At the last day He shall call all that are in the graves, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of damnation (John 5:29). The raisings of Scripture are the dawn-light of that morning—real, but partial; pledges of a glory that does not fade.

etymology: From the Sermon on the Mount; the wild flowers Christ set forth as a rebuke to anxious care (Matt 6:28).
biblical_def: The lilies of the field are the wild flowers of Galilee which the Lord Jesus set before His disciples in the Sermon on the Mount as a rebuke to anxious care and a lesson in the providence of God. Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: and yet, He said, Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. If God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall He not much more clothe His children, O ye of little faith? The lesson is not idleness, for the birds He bids us behold do gather and the lilies do grow, but freedom from the corroding anxiety that forgets the Father’s care. The disciple is to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, trusting that all these things—food and raiment and the needs of the body—shall be added unto him, and to take no anxious thought for the morrow. The dictionary honors the lilies of the field as the Lord’s tender argument from the lesser to the greater: that the God who arrays the perishing flower in beauty surpassing Solomon will surely clothe and feed the children He has redeemed, and that anxious care is therefore both needless and a reproach to faith.
webster_summary: The wild flowers Christ set forth in the Sermon on the Mount to rebuke anxious care and teach trust in the Father’s providence: consider the lilies, how they grow.

corruption_summary: The lilies are made an excuse for idleness or a mere nature-sentiment; Christ teaches trust in providence and the seeking of His kingdom above anxious care.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One corruption turns the lilies into a charter for idleness, as though the Lord forbade work and provision; another reduces the saying to a vague nature-sentiment about stopping to appreciate flowers. Both miss the point. The Lord does not forbid labor—the very lilies grow and the birds gather—but He forbids the anxious, faithless care that lives as if there were no Father in heaven.

The principle to recover is the providence of God as the cure for anxiety. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if God arrays the perishing grass in beauty surpassing Solomon (Matt 6:29), He will surely clothe His blood-bought children, O ye of little faith. The disciple is therefore to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, with the promise that all these things shall be added (Matt 6:33), and to take no anxious thought for the morrow (Matt 6:34). Anxiety is here named not merely as a burden but as a reproach to faith in a Father who feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies.

etymology: From the saying of Christ in Luke 12:24, bidding His disciples behold the ravens that God feeds.
biblical_def: Consider the ravens is the Lord’s saying in Luke, the companion to the lilies of the field, by which He bids His disciples cast away anxious care by beholding the providence of God toward the birds. Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls? The raven is fitly chosen, an unclean bird under the law, scavenging and despised, yet the same God who once commanded the ravens to feed Elijah by the brook Cherith opens His hand and feeds them still, who cry unto Him for their meat. If God so cares for the unclean raven that neither sows nor stores, how much more will He provide for His own children, of more value than many sparrows. The saying teaches not improvidence but trust—a freedom from the anxious, grasping care that betrays unbelief in the Father’s goodness. The dictionary honors this word as the Lord’s tender argument from the bird to the believer: that the God who feeds the young ravens when they cry will not forget the children He has bought with the blood of His Son, and that anxious thought is therefore the fruit of little faith.
webster_summary: Christ’s saying bidding His disciples behold the ravens God feeds, that they cast away anxious care: how much more are ye better than the fowls?

corruption_summary: The saying is taken to forbid prudent provision or reduced to mere sentiment; Christ teaches trust in the Father’s providence against anxious unbelief.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the reading that turns the saying into a command to make no provision at all, or into a mere sentimental appreciation of nature. Scripture elsewhere commends the ant that gathers in summer and warns that he who provides not for his own has denied the faith. The Lord does not here forbid labor or prudence; He forbids the anxious, faithless care that lives as though there were no God who feeds the ravens.

The principle to recover is the fatherly providence of God as the ground of peace. The argument moves from the unclean raven, which neither sows nor stores yet is fed by God (Luke 12:24; Psa 147:9), to the children of the kingdom, of far more value. The God who hears the young ravens when they cry (Job 38:41) will not forget His blood-bought people. So the Lord seals the lesson with comfort: Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32). Anxious care is rebuked, and trust in the Father is restored.

etymology: From Isaiah 61:2, quoted by Christ in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:19); the year of the Lord’s favour.
biblical_def: The acceptable year of the Lord is the year of God’s favour proclaimed in the gospel, the phrase of Isaiah which the Lord Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth and applied to Himself: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Closing the book, He declared, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears. The phrase echoes the year of jubilee, when debts were released, slaves set free, and inheritances restored; in Christ the true jubilee is come, the day of salvation, the time accepted in which God receives sinners through His Son. Notably the Lord stopped His reading before the words the day of vengeance of our God, for His first coming opened the era of grace; the day of vengeance awaits His return. The dictionary honors the acceptable year of the Lord as the gospel age itself, the open door of mercy now proclaimed to the captives and the bruised, and warns that this accepted time is also a limited time: behold, now is the accepted year; today, if ye will hear His voice, harden not your hearts.
webster_summary: The year of God’s favour proclaimed in the gospel, the jubilee fulfilled in Christ, who read Isaiah 61 at Nazareth and declared it fulfilled that day.

corruption_summary: The acceptable year is read as a program of merely social liberation; Scripture proclaims the gospel jubilee of salvation in Christ, an open but limited day of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chief corruption is the reduction of the acceptable year to a program of social and economic liberation only, as if Christ’s mission at Nazareth were chiefly political. The jubilee imagery is real—release, liberty, restoration—but its fulfilment in Christ is the deliverance of sinners from the bondage of sin and death, the healing of the brokenhearted, and the opening of the prison of guilt. To flatten the acceptable year into mere social reform is to miss the salvation it proclaims.

The principle to recover is twofold. First, the acceptable year is the gospel age itself, the open door of mercy: Christ stopped His reading before the day of vengeance (Isa 61:2), for His first coming opened the era of grace, and the vengeance awaits His return. Second, the accepted time is a limited time. Paul presses the urgency: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2). The acceptable year is open today, but it will close; the gospel call is therefore, Today, if ye will hear His voice, harden not your hearts.

etymology: From the Gospel narrative; the forty-day testing of Christ by Satan in the wilderness after His baptism.
biblical_def: The temptation in the wilderness is the forty-day testing of the Lord Jesus by Satan, immediately after His baptism, when the Spirit led Him up into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil. Having fasted forty days and forty nights, He was an hungred, and the tempter came with three assaults: to command the stones to be made bread, distrusting the Father’s provision; to cast Himself from the temple pinnacle, presuming on the Father’s protection; and to win the kingdoms of the world by worshipping Satan, forsaking the Father’s appointed way of the cross. To each the Lord answered, It is written, wielding the words of Deuteronomy against the foe, and so overcame. As the last Adam, He stood where the first Adam fell, and where Israel had failed forty years in the wilderness; tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin. His victory is not merely an example but a substitution: the Captain of salvation, made perfect through sufferings, conquers the tempter on behalf of His people. The dictionary honors the temptation in the wilderness as the opening battle of the Lord’s warfare, the proof of His sinless obedience, and the ground of the believer’s help, for in that He himself hath suffered being tempted, He is able to succour them that are tempted.
webster_summary: The forty-day testing of Christ by Satan after His baptism; the last Adam, answering It is written, overcame where Adam and Israel had fallen.

corruption_summary: The temptation is read as inner psychological struggle or mere moral example; Scripture shows a real assault by a real Satan, overcome by the sinless last Adam.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One corruption psychologizes the temptation into Jesus wrestling with His own inner doubts, denying the real and personal adversary; another reduces it to a bare moral example of resisting temptation, severed from its place in redemption. The text resists both: Jesus was led up to be tempted of the devil (Matt 4:1), a real and malignant foe, and His victory was that of the last Adam standing where the first had fallen.

The principle to recover is the substitutionary and sympathetic character of Christ’s victory. He overcame not as a private individual but as the Captain of His people’s salvation, conquering the tempter on their behalf and earning the righteousness imputed to them. And because He was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15), He is a merciful and faithful high priest, able to succour them that are tempted. His answer to every assault—It is written—is also the believer’s weapon: the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

etymology: From the Gospel narrative; the question of paying tribute to Caesar, answered by Christ (Matt 22:21).
biblical_def: The tribute to Caesar is the question the Pharisees and Herodians brought to ensnare the Lord Jesus: Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not? The trap was sharp—if He said yes, He offended the people who chafed under Rome; if no, He could be accused of sedition. But the Lord, perceiving their wickedness, called for the tribute money, asked whose image and superscription it bore, and when they answered, Caesar’s, gave the answer that has guided the church ever since: Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. The coin bearing Caesar’s image was owed to Caesar; but man, bearing the image of God, owes himself wholly to God. The saying establishes the lawful but limited authority of the civil magistrate, to whom the Christian owes taxes, honour, and obedience in his sphere, while reserving to God the absolute allegiance of the conscience and the worship that is His alone. Civil obedience and supreme loyalty to God are not rivals when each is rendered in its place. The dictionary honors this word as the charter of the two spheres of authority: the magistrate is God’s minister, to be obeyed for conscience’ sake, yet never to be given the worship and ultimate obedience that belong to God alone, for we must obey God rather than men.
webster_summary: Christ’s answer to the trap about paying tribute: render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s.

Tell us therefore, What thinkest thou? Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?
Rom 13:1

Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: The saying is twisted into a wall against any faith in public life, or into a charter for unlimited state power; Christ set two spheres of authority, God’s being supreme.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond two opposite distortions. The first wields Render unto Caesar as a wall of separation banishing faith from public life, as though the things of God were a private hobby with no claim on the civil sphere. The second runs the other way, making the saying a charter for unlimited state power, to which the Christian owes whatever Caesar demands. Both misread the Lord, who divided the spheres but did not make them equal.

The principle to recover is the ordered, limited, and accountable authority of the magistrate under God. The coin bearing Caesar’s image is owed to Caesar; the believer pays his taxes and honours the higher powers, which are ordained of God (Rom 13:1). But man bears the image of God, and owes God himself—his worship, his conscience, his ultimate allegiance—which no Caesar may claim. When the magistrate demands what belongs to God alone, the rule is plain: we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Caesar’s sphere is real but bounded; God’s claim is total.
roots_summary: From the Gospels; Christ’s answer to the tribute trap, dividing the spheres: Caesar’s things to Caesar, God’s things to God.

etymology: The half-shekel paid by every Israelite for the service of the sanctuary; in the Gospels, the tribute money of Matthew 17.
biblical_def: The temple tax was the half-shekel required of every Israelite male for the service and upkeep of the sanctuary, rooted in the atonement money of Exodus, where every man numbered gave a ransom for his soul, the rich no more and the poor no less than half a shekel, a memorial before the LORD. In the Gospel of Matthew, those who received this tribute money asked Peter whether his Master paid it; and the Lord taught Peter a deep lesson by a question: of whom do the kings of the earth take custom, of their own children, or of strangers? Peter answered, Of strangers; and Jesus said, Then are the children free—for He, the Son of the God whose house the temple was, owed no tax for His Father’s house. Yet lest they should offend, He bade Peter cast a hook into the sea, and in the mouth of the first fish was found a coin sufficient to pay for them both. The scene reveals both the dignity of the Son, free in His Father’s house, and His gracious condescension, paying what He did not owe, and His sovereign provision drawn even from the sea. The dictionary honors the temple tax narrative as a window into the Sonship of Christ, His voluntary humility, and the lordship by which He provides for His own.

corruption_summary: The episode is treated as a mere wonder-tale or a lesson in civic duty; it reveals the Sonship, condescension, and sovereign provision of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the flattening of the scene into either a quaint wonder-tale about a coin in a fish or a bare lesson in paying one’s dues. Both miss the weight of the Lord’s teaching. The point turns on Sonship: the children of the king are free from His tribute, and Jesus, the Son of the God whose house the temple was, owed nothing for His Father’s house (Matt 17:26). The episode is first a revelation of who He is.

The principle to recover is the union of Christ’s dignity, His condescension, and His provision. Though free, He paid the tax lest He should offend (Matt 17:27), foreshadowing the deeper grace by which, though He was rich, for our sakes He became poor (2 Cor 8:9), paying a debt He did not owe. And He provided the very coin by His sovereign lordship, drawing it from the mouth of a fish in the sea—a small parable of the Lord who owns the cattle on a thousand hills and provides for His own from sources no man foresees. The humble half-shekel becomes a window into the Son who stoops and the Lord who supplies.
roots_summary: The half-shekel for the sanctuary, rooted in Exodus; in Matthew 17 the free Son pays it in condescension, providing the coin from a fish.

etymology: The phrase of Christ at the Last Supper for the cup of the Lord’s Supper (Matt 26:29).
biblical_def: The fruit of the vine is the Lord’s own phrase for the cup of the Supper which He instituted on the night He was betrayed. Taking the cup, He gave thanks, and gave it to His disciples, saying, This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins; and He added, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom. The cup, the fruit of the vine, is the appointed sign and seal of the new covenant in His blood, set forth in the Lord’s Supper for the perpetual remembrance of His death until He come. By it the believer feeds, not with the mouth of the body but by faith, upon the crucified and risen Christ, who is spiritually present to nourish His people, against both the Roman error that the elements are changed into His body and blood and the bare memorialism that empties the Supper of His real spiritual presence. The Lord’s word also looks forward, to the marriage supper of the Lamb, when He shall drink it new with His people in the Father’s kingdom. The dictionary honors the fruit of the vine as the cup of the new covenant, the sign and seal of remission through the blood of Christ, and the pledge of the feast to come.

The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
corruption_summary: The cup is misread as transubstantiated blood or as a bare token; Scripture sets it forth as the sign and seal of the new covenant, with Christ spiritually present to faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions surround the cup. On one side, the Roman doctrine of transubstantiation holds that the fruit of the vine is changed into the very blood of Christ, so that the sign is swallowed up in a supposed miracle and the Supper becomes a propitiatory sacrifice repeated by the priest—a denial that Christ’s one offering was finished upon the cross. On the other side, a bare memorialism empties the cup of all but remembrance, denying that Christ is truly present to nourish His people, and so reduces the seal of the covenant to a mere sign and the means of grace to a bare token.

The principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine of the Supper. The cup is the new testament in His blood (1 Cor 11:25), the communion of the blood of Christ (1 Cor 10:16): a true sign and seal in which the believer, by faith and through the Spirit, feeds upon the crucified and risen Christ who is spiritually present to His people. The elements are not changed, yet they are not empty; they convey Christ to the believing soul as surely as the bread feeds the body. And the cup looks beyond itself to the marriage supper of the Lamb, when the Lord shall drink it new with His own in the Father’s kingdom (Matt 26:29).
